title: The Sambation and the Seventy-Two Names: Abulafia from Zaragoza to Comino
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Father's House: Zaragoza and Tudela

stops.name: Zaragoza, born in the year five thousand
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com; English Wikipedia), which is the Hebrew year 5000. Month and day are unrecorded and defaulted to 01-01. No source gives a street, a synagogue, or a house; the coordinate is the city.
stops.campa: Abraham ben Samuel Abulafia is born at Zaragoza, in the Jewish quarter of the Aragonese capital, in the Hebrew year five thousand. The round number is not lost on him; he will spend his life reading dates as arguments. His father Samuel takes charge of the boy's Bible and Talmud himself, and the household keeps no other teacher on record. Other houses of the name Abulafia sit in Toledo, courtiers and Talmudists of considerable weight, and no pedigree anyone has found joins them to this one.
suggested_refs: The Jewish quarter of medieval Zaragoza, largest Jewish community of the Crown of Aragon
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)

stops.name: Tudela, the family crosses into Navarre
stops.date_confidence: The move is attested but undated: Encyclopedia.com gives only 'during his childhood', before the father's death in 1258. The year 1248 is an ordering device and is not in any source.
stops.campa: The family crosses the Ebro into the Kingdom of Navarre and settles at Tudela, a walled town of gardens and irrigation channels where Jews, Muslims and Christians hold their quarters within a few streets of one another. Abraham is still a child when they come over, and the sources fix no closer year than that. Here Samuel finishes the boy's schooling in the two Laws, and he goes on teaching him until the year he dies. Nothing of Abraham's own hand survives from these years, and no source names anyone else who taught him.
suggested_refs: The juderia of Tudela on the Ebro, under Navarrese protection in the thirteenth century
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)
Jewish Virtual Library, 'Abraham ben Samuel Abulafia'

stops.name: Tudela, the death of Samuel
stops.date_confidence: Attested that his father died when Abraham was eighteen, which fixes the year at 1258. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Samuel dies at Tudela in 1258, which is the one date the sources fix by counting back from his son's age. Abraham is eighteen, and the schooling stops where it stood: Bible and Talmud from one man, in a provincial town, with no academy behind it and no chain of masters to name. No source gives the place of the grave. None gives the mother a name at all. What the son does for the next two years nobody wrote down. When he appears again he is twenty, and he is leaving Iberia altogether, not for a school and not for a trade.
suggested_refs: Tudela's Jewish cemetery, unlocated in the sources for this family
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)
Jewish Virtual Library, 'Abraham ben Samuel Abulafia'

stops.name: Barcelona, embarking for the Land of Israel
stops.date_confidence: The departure at age twenty in 1260 is attested. The port is not: no source names where he took ship, and Barcelona is inference from the Aragonese geography. Month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: At twenty he goes down to the sea and takes ship for the Land of Israel. He is not going on pilgrimage. He is going to find the Sambation, the river of Jewish travel lore that runs with stones six days a week and rests on the Sabbath, and beyond it the Ten Tribes carried off by Assyria and never accounted for since. Every literate Jew in Aragon knows the story; Abulafia treats it as an itinerary and takes ship on it. No source names the port he sailed from.
suggested_refs: The Sambation of rabbinic and medieval travel lore, the river of stones beyond which the Ten Tribes were said to live
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)
Jewish Virtual Library, 'Abraham ben Samuel Abulafia'

stops.name: Acre, the road east closes
stops.date_confidence: Attested that he reached Akko in 1260 and went no further; month is an ordering device. The Mongol-Mamluk war of that year is context and not testimony: Wikipedia says only that he reached Akko before returning to Europe, and gives no cause for the turn-back.
stops.campa: He reaches Acre, the last great Crusader port on the Syrian coast, and can go no further. That year the Mongols and the Mamluks are fighting for possession of the whole Levant, and the roads inland belong to armies. The sources say he got as far as Akko and turned back; none of them says why, and none says how long he stayed or whether he saw anything of the country behind the port. He does not find the Sambation. Nobody has ever found the Sambation. He turns west again. He is twenty.
suggested_refs: The Crusader port of Acre in 1260, thirty-one years before its fall
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Abraham ben Samuel Abulafia'

stops.name: Greece, a marriage with no name in it
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The marriage in Greece appears in one biographical notice (Encyclopedia.com) and is not carried by the Jewish Encyclopedia or the Jewish Virtual Library entries. No city is named; the coordinate is a central-mainland placeholder, not a landmark. The year is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Working back toward Italy through Greece, he marries. The notice is a single line in one biographical entry: a wife, in Greece, and then nothing. Her name is not given, nor her family, nor whether she is still living when he is imprisoned at Rome twenty years later, nor whether she crosses to Sicily with him. He will write some thirty surviving books about the interior life and mention her in none of them. Whether she is with him for any of the road that follows, no source says.
suggested_refs: Encyclopaedia Judaica's single-line notice of the Greek marriage, uncorroborated elsewhere
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)

stops.name: Capua, the Guide of the Perplexed under Rabbi Hillel
stops.date_confidence: Encyclopaedia Judaica gives 'the early 1260s' and states flatly that the teacher was R. Hillel of Verona; the Jewish Encyclopedia calls him only 'a philosopher and physician named Hillel'. The year 1262 and the month are reconstruction for ordering, not attested.
stops.campa: At Capua, in the Lombard and Norman country north of Naples, he sits down with a teacher he calls Rabbi Hillel and reads the Guide of the Perplexed. Maimonides has been dead sixty years and his book is still the argument the Jewish world is having with itself: whether prophecy is a natural faculty of a prepared intellect or a gift interrupted. Abulafia reads it as a manual. He will spend the next thirty years turning Maimonidean prophecy into something a man can sit down and practise on a given evening, with the letters in front of him and his own breath to work with.
suggested_refs: Maimonides, Guide of the Perplexed, completed at Fustat in 1190
Hillel ben Samuel of Verona, physician and Maimonidean, the identification given by Encyclopaedia Judaica
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)

segments.name: The Thirty-First Year: Barcelona and Castile

stops.name: Barcelona, the thirty-first year
stops.date_confidence: Encyclopaedia Judaica dates the Barcelona period to 1270; Wikipedia gives 'at the age of thirty-one', which is 1271. Both are in circulation and neither is preferred here; read as c. 1270-71. No source names a house, a street or a synagogue, so the coordinate is the medieval city centre.
stops.campa: He is about thirty-one and back in Barcelona when something happens that he treats afterward as the hinge of his life. He begins working on Sefer Yetzirah, the Book of Formation, the small ancient text that builds the world out of ten numbers and twenty-two letters, and he receives what he describes as a revelation carrying messianic weight. Until now he has read philosophy in Italy and failed to find a river in Palestine. The year is either 1270 or 1271. The sources that give it do not agree, and neither reckoning has ever been settled against the other.
suggested_refs: Sefer Yetzirah, the Book of Formation, and its thirteenth-century Catalan commentators
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)

stops.name: Barcelona, Baruch Togarmi and the Book of Formation
stops.date_confidence: The sources disagree on the nature of the tie. Encyclopaedia Judaica says he 'studied under Baruch Togarmi' at Barcelona in 1270, which is personal instruction; English Wikipedia says only that Togarmi was the most important representative of that kind of Kabbalah, which is textual influence. The disagreement is left standing. Month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The Kabbalah he takes up at Barcelona is not the Kabbalah of the ten sefirot that the Catalan masters are building. It works on the letters themselves: combination, permutation, the vocalization of the Names, tzeruf. Its principal document is Baruch Togarmi's commentary on Sefer Yetzirah, and Abulafia takes it up here. Whether Togarmi taught him face to face or only on the page is what the sources disagree about. He is candid enough elsewhere about what he saw in his visions. He never says which it was.
suggested_refs: Baruch Togarmi, Maftehot ha-Kabbalah, commentary on Sefer Yetzirah
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)

stops.name: Barcelona, Sefer ha-Ge'ullah
stops.date_confidence: The year 1273 is attested for the work by Encyclopaedia Judaica and Wikipedia. The city of composition is not given anywhere; Barcelona is inference from the surrounding chronology and should be read as unlocated. Month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: He writes Sefer ha-Ge'ullah, the Book of Redemption, and it is a commentary on the Guide of the Perplexed. This is the pattern for the rest of his working life: the mystic does not turn away from the philosopher, he annotates him. Two more commentaries on the same book will follow, Hayyei ha-Nefesh and Sitrei Torah, until the Guide has been read three times over and converted, chapter by chapter, into a practice. Maimonides wrote it to quiet exactly this kind of reader.
suggested_refs: Sefer ha-Ge'ullah (1273), first of the three Abulafian commentaries on the Guide
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)
Sefaria topic page, 'Abraham ben Samuel Abulafia'

stops.name: Castile, the teaching circuit
stops.date_confidence: Mid-1270s. Both Encyclopaedia Judaica and Wikipedia state the Castilian teaching and name the two pupils directly, so the fact is attested; the itinerary is not, no city is fixed, and the coordinate is a central-Castile placeholder. Gikatilla's own surviving works do not name Abulafia as his teacher.
stops.campa: He goes to Castile and teaches, moving between towns rather than settling in one. Two pupils are named in the sources: Moses ben Simeon of Burgos, and Joseph Gikatilla, called his most important disciple, who will carry the letter-technique into the circle around Moses de Leon where the Zohar is being written. Gikatilla's own books never name Abulafia as his teacher. The claim rests on Abulafia's word and on what the two men's pages have in common.
suggested_refs: Joseph ben Abraham Gikatilla, Ginnat Egoz, built on letter-permutation and gematria
Moses ben Simeon of Burgos, Castilian kabbalist
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)
moses_de_leon.journey.json, 'Guadalajara, Gikatilla and the two Kabbalahs'

stops.name: Castile, Hayyei ha-Nefesh, the second commentary
stops.date_confidence: The work is attested as the second of the three commentaries on the Guide, but no source fetched gives it a year or a place. It is placed here only to order the series between Sefer ha-Ge'ullah (1273) and Sitrei Torah (1280). Both the date and the Castile coordinate are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Somewhere in these Castilian years he writes Hayyei ha-Nefesh, Life of the Soul, the second of the three commentaries on the Guide. No source gives it a year or a town. It sits between the Book of Redemption and Sitrei Torah by the logic of a series and by nothing else. A good deal of his bibliography sits that way: the titles are known and their order is known, and the dates and the places are mostly gone. The manuscripts that carry it were copied later, by hands that did not sign.
suggested_refs: Hayyei ha-Nefesh, second commentary on the Guide, undated and unplaced in the reference literature
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)

segments.name: Greece Again, and the Books He Calls Prophetic

stops.name: Patras, the first of the prophetic books
stops.date_confidence: Attested independently by the Jewish Encyclopedia, the Jewish Virtual Library and Wikipedia, all naming Patras and 1279. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01. An earlier draft of this research placed teaching at Thebes in 1275; no source supports Thebes and that stop was dropped.
stops.campa: In Patras, on the Gulf of Corinth, he begins the books he calls prophetic. The first is Sefer ha-Yashar, the Book of the Upright, and he does not claim to have composed it in the ordinary way; he claims it was given. A series of these follows over the next decade, and he goes on adding to it long after this first one brings nothing about. All of them are lost except Sefer ha-Ot, which he will write on Comino eight years from now. Of the others there remain the titles, and the places in his surviving books where he refers back to his own work.
suggested_refs: Sefer ha-Yashar (Patras, 1279), first and lost of the prophetic books
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Abraham ben Samuel Abulafia'

stops.name: Trani, the road home through Apulia
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia states that he made his way through Trani back to Capua in that same year, 1279. The month is an ordering device and is not attested.
stops.campa: He crosses to the heel of Italy and works north through Trani, a port on the Adriatic with one of the oldest Jewish communities in the south, its synagogues built in stone and its school of some standing. He does not stay. The whole Greek and Apulian passage of 1279 is a line of towns in a single sentence in the reference books: Patras, Trani, Capua. He is thirty-nine. The road from Trani to Capua crosses the whole width of the peninsula, and he covers it before the year is out.
suggested_refs: The medieval synagogues of Trani, among the oldest surviving in southern Italy
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)

stops.name: Capua, four young students
stops.date_confidence: Attested that he returned to Capua in 1279-80 and taught four students there. The often-repeated phrase 'four precious stones' appears in none of the encyclopedia entries or the Wikipedia article and is not treated as a quotation here. Month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Back at Capua, where he read the Guide as a young man, he gathers four students and teaches them his own way of reading it. The sources call them four young students and nothing further. A phrase about four precious stones circulates in modern retellings and appears in none of the reference entries. Their names are not given, nor their ages, nor what became of any of them afterward, and nothing from their hands survives to say what they made of it. He is forty. Within the year he leaves them and goes north to Rome.
suggested_refs: The Jewish community of Capua under Angevin rule
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)

stops.name: Capua, Sitrei Torah for the four
stops.date_confidence: The year 1280 is attested by Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Sefaria topic listing; the month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: For these four he writes Sitrei Torah, Secrets of the Torah, the third and largest of his commentaries on the Guide. It is a teaching text, made for men sitting in front of him, and it carries the practice as well as the doctrine: how the letters are to be combined, what the body does while they are being combined, what is to be feared. It is the longest thing he ever writes about the Guide, and what a Spanish Jew in Campania is setting down in it, for four young men whose names nobody recorded, is a technique for inducing prophecy on purpose. The copy scholars work from is at Paris, MS 774.
suggested_refs: Sitrei Torah (1280), MS Paris 774, largest of the three commentaries on the Guide
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)
Sefaria topic page, 'Abraham ben Samuel Abulafia'

stops.name: Capua, the manual of the seventy-two-letter Name
stops.date_confidence: The year 1280 is attested; the month is an ordering device. Wikipedia and the Sefaria listing give the work without a city, and Capua is inference from the teaching circle of the same year.
stops.campa: The same year he finishes Hayyei ha-Olam ha-Ba, Life of the World to Come, and it is a manual: circles of letters to be drawn, tables of vocalization, the seventy-two-letter Name derived from three consecutive verses of Exodus read forward, backward and forward again, the order in which the syllables are pronounced and the breath taken. It assumes a reader alone in a room at night, working down the tables and expecting to be answered. Of everything he wrote, it is the book that was copied most.
stops.quote: And consider his reply, answering as though you yourself had answered yourself
stops.quote_source: Abraham Abulafia, Hayyei ha-Olam ha-Ba (Life of the World to Come), English translation as quoted in the Wikipedia article 'Abraham Abulafia'
suggested_refs: Hayyei ha-Olam ha-Ba (1280), the seventy-two triplets of Exodus 14:19-21 and the vocalization circles
sources: Sefaria topic page, 'Abraham ben Samuel Abulafia'

segments.name: Rome: the Pope Who Died First

stops.name: Rome, the approach to the curia
stops.date_confidence: The 1280 journey to Rome is attested by all three reference entries. The month is an ordering device. The purpose is stated flatly in the sources as an attempt to convert Nicholas III to Judaism; a softer framing as a debate about redemption is a later gloss and is not used here.
stops.campa: He goes to Rome, in the summer of 1280, to convert the pope. The sources say it plainly and do not soften it: he means to bring Nicholas III to Judaism and to settle with him the meaning of redemption. He is a Spanish Jew of forty with no office and no protection, and no community behind him that any source names, walking toward the most heavily guarded man in Latin Christendom. Nothing in his own writing suggests he thought it unlikely to work. The pope is not in Rome. He is at the family castle at Soriano, north of the city.
suggested_refs: Pope Nicholas III (Giovanni Gaetano Orsini), r. 1277-1280
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Abraham ben Samuel Abulafia'

stops.name: Soriano nel Cimino, the stake at the inner gate
stops.date_confidence: 22 August 1280 is the attested date of Nicholas III's death at the Orsini castle in the diocese of Viterbo; the cause is given as apoplectic stroke in some accounts and heart attack in others. Wikipedia's Nicholas III article puts Abulafia at Soriano that same day; Wikipedia's Abulafia article says he went on the day before Rosh Hashanah, which for 5041 falls on 26 August, four days after the pope died. The two datings cannot both be right and neither is preferred here.
stops.campa: The pope, hearing what is coming, gives orders that the fanatic is to be burned as soon as he reaches Soriano, and the stake is put up close to the inner gate of the castle. Abulafia comes on anyway. On the night before he arrives Nicholas III dies suddenly at the Orsini castle, of a stroke or a heart attack depending on the account, and the men at the gate have a stake, a warrant and no pope. Two dates for his arrival stand in the record, 22 August and the eve of Rosh Hashanah four days later, and they cannot both be true.
suggested_refs: The Orsini castle at Soriano nel Cimino, summer residence of Nicholas III
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Pope Nicholas III', quoting Abulafia's biography

stops.name: Rome, four weeks with the Minorites
stops.date_confidence: Four weeks is given independently by the Jewish Encyclopedia and by Wikipedia; a two-week figure circulates in one modern scholarly retelling and is noted as a minority reading. No source fetched names which Franciscan house held him, so the coordinate is the city and not the site. Month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Back in Rome he is taken by the Franciscan Minorites and held four weeks. No charge survives, no trial, no sentence. Two reference accounts give the same four weeks and then his release; one modern retelling halves it to two. No source names the house that held him. He walks out at the end of it and out of the Papal States, and never approaches a Christian authority again. Why the Minorites let a man go who had come to convert their pope, nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: The Franciscan Minorite houses of Rome in 1280, none identified in the sources as his prison
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Abraham ben Samuel Abulafia'

segments.name: Sicily: Prophet, Messiah, and the Letters from Barcelona

stops.name: Messina, the crossing to Sicily
stops.date_confidence: Attested that he relocated to Sicily and was active at Messina from about 1281 through 1291. The precise year of the crossing is not fixed; month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: He crosses to Sicily and settles at Messina, on the strait between the island and Calabria, and stays for the last decade of his life. It is the longest he remains anywhere after childhood. Sicily under the Angevins is a country of Greek, Arabic, Latin and Hebrew spoken in the same streets, and its Jewish communities are old, wealthy and self-governing. He is forty-one when he lands. The technique is worked out and written down by now; the claim about himself he has not yet made in public.
suggested_refs: The Jewish community of Messina in the late thirteenth century
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)

stops.name: Messina, the circle and the technique
stops.date_confidence: The Messina teaching circle is attested for the period 1281-1291; this stop's year is an ordering device. Sefer ha-Kheshek, from which the quote is taken, is undated and unplaced in the sources fetched.
stops.campa: At Messina disciples come to him and he teaches the practice directly: the letters, the vocalizations, the postures, the breathing, and the figure a man is to imagine sitting opposite him, waiting to be questioned. The instruction is precise about the body. It says what will shake and what will heat, and it says that the voice which answers is to be understood as the practitioner's own and not his own at once. It requires no synagogue and no quorum. A man sits down in a room with the alphabet in front of him and begins.
stops.quote: [A]nd sit as though a man is standing before you and waiting for you to speak with him; and he is ready to answer you concerning whatever you may ask him...
stops.quote_source: Abraham Abulafia, Sefer ha-Kheshek, MS New York JTS 1801, fol. 9a; also MS British Library 749, fols. 12a-12b; English translation as quoted in the Wikipedia article 'Abraham Abulafia'
suggested_refs: Sefer ha-Kheshek, MS New York JTS 1801 and MS British Library 749

stops.name: Messina, prophet, messiah, son of God
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia attaches these self-descriptions to the Messina period, 1281-1291, and not to any single year or to Palermo. The year here orders the segment. The redemption date of 1290 is drawn from his own calculations as reported in the reference literature.
stops.campa: In these Messina years he begins saying in the open what the prophetic books had said obliquely: that he is a prophet, that he is the messiah, and, in some formulations, that he is a son of God. The claim is attached by the sources to Messina and to no single year in the decade. He has a date as well. His reading of the numbers puts the redemption in 1290, nine years off. Sicilian Jews take sides. Some follow him. Some write to the mainland about him, and the letters they send will come back as a ruling out of Barcelona.
suggested_refs: Abulafia's messianic calculation for 1290, reported across the reference literature
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)

stops.name: Messina, Or ha-Sekhel and the joining of the intellects
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction throughout. Wikipedia lists Or ha-Sekhel among his handbooks with no date, no dedicatee and no city; the dedication to a pupil called Nathan the Wise appears in none of the sources fetched and is not asserted here. Both the 1283 date and the Messina location are ordering devices.
stops.campa: He writes Or ha-Sekhel, Light of the Intellect, and in it says what the whole technique is for. Prophecy is not a message handed to a man from outside himself. It is the joining of a human intellect to the divine intellect until the two are one thing and the difference between the one who speaks and the one spoken to gives way. The machinery of the argument is Aristotelian and its vocabulary is Jewish, which is one reason the philosophers and the Talmudists find him equally intolerable. No source fetched gives the book a year, a city or a dedicatee.
stops.quote: The connection of human existence with the divine existence during intellection, which is identical with the intellect in [its] existence, until he and He become one [entity].
stops.quote_source: Abraham Abulafia, Or ha-Sekhel, translated by Elliot R. Wolfson, 'Jewish Mysticism: A Philosophical Overview', in History of Jewish Philosophy (Routledge, 1996), excerpted at My Jewish Learning
suggested_refs: Vat. ebr. 597, an illuminated Italian manuscript of Sefer Or ha-Sekhel, mid-to-late fifteenth century, Vatican Library
sources: Elliot R. Wolfson, 'Abraham Abulafia and Ecstatic Kabbalah', My Jewish Learning
Center for Jewish Art manuscript database, record 1118

stops.name: Palermo, the community writes to Barcelona
stops.date_confidence: Attested that the Jewish leaders of Palermo appealed to Solomon ben Abraham ibn Adret and that he answered with a letter condemning Abulafia's conduct, printed as responsum 1:548. The year 1285 is the conventional date and is not tightly fixed in the sources. The phrase 'villain and liar' circulates in modern accounts and is not in the Jewish Encyclopedia or Jewish Virtual Library entries; it is not quoted here.
stops.campa: The Jewish leaders of Palermo, with a man in their island calling himself prophet and messiah and gathering students, write to Barcelona for a ruling. The letter that comes back is from Solomon ben Abraham ibn Adret, the Rashba, the most authoritative legal voice in Aragon, and it condemns Abulafia's conduct as forcefully as the genre permits. It does not stay in Palermo. Copies go out to communities across the western Mediterranean and are acted on. The letter is still in print among the Rashba's responsa, as number 1:548.
suggested_refs: Solomon ben Abraham ibn Adret, Responsa 1:548, against the self-proclaimed prophet in Sicily
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Abraham ben Samuel Abulafia'

stops.name: Sicily, the reply to the Rashba
stops.date_confidence: The epistle Ve-Zot li-Yehudah is attested as his answer to Ibn Adret's attack; no source fetched gives a month, and none gives a place of composition. Both the month and the Messina coordinate are ordering devices.
stops.campa: He answers. The reply, Ve-Zot li-Yehudah, defends the Kabbalah of the Names against men he regards as mere Talmudists, competent in the law and deaf to the letters. He does not retract the messianic claim and does not apologize for the prophecy. Against the most respected legal authority in Aragon he argues that the masters of the Talmud hold the smaller portion of the Torah, and that the letters, which are older than the law, hold the larger. Nobody in Palermo is persuaded. Whether Ibn Adret ever read the reply, no source says.
suggested_refs: Ve-Zot li-Yehudah, printed by Adolf Jellinek in Auswahl kabbalistischer Mystik (Leipzig, 1853), one of the first modern printings of any Abulafia text

stops.name: Messina, Otzar Eden Ganuz
stops.date_confidence: Encyclopaedia Judaica and Wikipedia both date the work 1285/6, so the year is attested within a one-year range; month and day defaulted to 01-01. No source gives a place of composition and the Messina coordinate is inference from the period. The quote below was carried in an earlier draft under a Sitrei Torah shelfmark; that attribution was wrong and is corrected here to Oxford MS 1580.
stops.campa: He writes Otzar Eden Ganuz, the Hidden Treasury of Eden, a long working commentary on Sefer Yetzirah and on the divine Names, surviving at Oxford as MS 1580, and the most detailed account he ever gives of what the practice does to a body. He is exact and he is not reassuring. He writes for a reader who intends to do exactly what the book says. The trembling comes first, then the heat, then something moving through the limbs that he compares to a rider on a racing horse, the rider glad and the horse shaking under him.
stops.quote: all your body will begin to tremble, and your limbs begin to shake, and you will fear a tremendous fear [...] and the body will tremble, like the rider who races the horse, who is glad and joyful, while the horse trembles beneath him.
stops.quote_source: Abraham Abulafia, Otzar Eden Ganuz, MS Oxford 1580, fols. 163b-164a (compare Hayyei ha-Olam ha-Ba, MS Oxford 1582, fol. 12a); English translation as quoted in the Wikipedia article 'Abraham Abulafia'
suggested_refs: Otzar Eden Ganuz (1285/6), MS Oxford 1580
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)

stops.name: Comino, the island exile
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia's Comino article gives 'from 1285 until some time after 1290' for his residence there. That span overlaps the Sicilian stops in the preceding segment, and no source explains how the two residences interleave; the overlap is left visible rather than resolved. Month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: He goes to Comino, a limestone island of a few hundred acres between Malta and Gozo, and lives there in conditions his own account calls distressed. It is a strange address for a man who has been teaching in the largest port cities of the Mediterranean: no community, no students on record, and hardly any fresh water on the island at all. He is about forty-five when he first goes over. The dates given for the Sicilian teaching and for the Comino exile overlap, and no source divides the years between them.
suggested_refs: The island of Comino between Malta and Gozo, uninhabited but for a handful of families in the thirteenth century

stops.name: Comino, the Book of the Sign
stops.date_confidence: The Jewish Encyclopedia and Wikipedia both give 1285-88 for the composition of Sefer ha-Ot on Comino; 1287 is a midpoint chosen to order the segment and is not itself attested. An earlier draft of this research fixed the work to 1285 alone, which is narrower than the sources allow.
stops.campa: On Comino he compiles Sefer ha-Ot, the Book of the Sign, the one prophetic book of his that survives. It is written in visions and it does not explain itself: a man out of the west with an army of twenty-two thousand, which is the number of the Hebrew letters, and a war fought inside the writer's own head between the ink and the blood. It is the book that is supposed to announce the redemption he has calculated, and he is writing it on an island with almost nobody on it. The sources put the composition between 1285 and 1288 and go no closer than that.
stops.quote: I saw a man coming from the west with a great army, the number of the warriors of his camp being twenty-two thousand men [...] And when I saw his face in the sight, I was astonished, and my heart trembled within me...
stops.quote_source: Abraham Abulafia, Sefer ha-Ot (Book of the Sign), pp. 81-82; English translation as quoted in the Wikipedia article 'Abraham Abulafia'
suggested_refs: Sefer ha-Ot, printed by Adolf Jellinek in the Graetz-Jubelschrift (1887)
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Abraham ben Samuel Abulafia'

stops.name: Sicily, the Key of the Torah
stops.date_confidence: The year 1289 is directly attested for Sefer Mafteah ha-Torah by both Encyclopaedia Judaica and Wikipedia. No source names a place of composition; the Messina coordinate is inference from his Sicilian base and should be read as unlocated. Month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: He finishes Mafteah ha-Torah, the Key of the Torah, a commentary running the length of the Pentateuch. It survives in substantial part, which most of the prophetic writing does not. The year is firm in two independent listings and the place is given in neither. The commentary keeps the Pentateuch's own order and reads every verse twice, once for what it says and once for what its letters can be made to say. By now he has written on the Guide three times, on Sefer Yetzirah at length, on the Names and on the technique itself. He is forty-nine, and he has two years of dated work left.
suggested_refs: Sefer Mafteah ha-Torah (1289), substantially extant Pentateuchal commentary
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)

stops.name: Sicily, the year 1290 arrives
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The messianic calculation for 1290 is reported in the reference literature; the passing of the year is not itself recorded anywhere, and no source preserves any comment of his on it. The Sicilian coordinate is inference: whether he spent that year on Sicily or on Comino is not established.
stops.campa: The year arrives. He has read it out of the numbers, written it into the prophetic books, defended it against the Rashba and staked the claim about himself on it, and the year comes and goes and nothing external happens at all. No source preserves what he said about it. He does not stop writing, he does not recant, and he does not leave the islands. He is fifty years old, and he has been carrying this number since Barcelona. Whether he set a second date after it, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The apocalyptic calculations of Abulafia's prophetic books, converging on 1290

stops.name: Comino, Imrei Shefer
stops.date_confidence: The year 1291 is attested by three independent listings as his last dated work. The place is contested: Wikipedia's Comino article states that both Sefer ha-Ot and his last work Imre Shefer were composed on Comino, while the project's own earlier draft placed it in Sicily. The Comino placement follows the source; the Sicilian placement was inference and is dropped. Month and day defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Imrei Shefer, Words of Beauty, is the last thing he writes that carries a date. In it he returns to what he has been saying since Barcelona twenty years earlier: that the letters in their forms are the clear mirror, and that a man who looks at them long enough will find that they answer. He is fifty-one, and has been writing for twenty years. His own count of his books stood at twenty-six; the modern catalogues put the figure higher. The manuscript is at Paris, BN 777.
stops.quote: And they [the letters], with their forms, are called the Clear Mirror, for all the forms having brightness and strong radiance are included in them. And one who gazes at them in their forms will discover their secrets and speak to them, and they will speak to him.
stops.quote_source: Abraham Abulafia, Imrei Shefer (Words of Beauty), MS Paris BN 777, fol. 49; English translation as quoted in the Wikipedia article 'Abraham Abulafia'
suggested_refs: Imrei Shefer (1291), MS Paris BN 777, printed by Adolf Jellinek in Philosophie und Kabbala (Leipzig)
sources: Jewish Virtual Library, 'Abraham ben Samuel Abulafia'

stops.name: Comino, all trace of him is lost
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the date is an ordering device only. There is no death notice, no grave, no burial record and no contemporary report of his death in any source consulted; 'died on Comino' is scholarly shorthand for the last place he can be proved to have been. A symbolic reburial on Malta in 2003 circulates in popular accounts and could not be confirmed against any primary source.
stops.campa: After Imrei Shefer there is nothing. No death notice, no grave, no colophon by a student, no letter reporting it, no responsum arguing about it. Tradition puts his death on Comino, and the tradition amounts to the last place anyone can prove he stood. Roughly thirty of his works survive whole or in fragments. His own count was twenty-six, of which he said twenty-two were prophetic. Twenty-two is the number of the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Nobody can now check the figure against the books, since the prophetic ones are the books that did not survive.
suggested_refs: Sifrei Rabbi Avraham Abulafia, ed. Amnon Gross, thirteen volumes (Jerusalem, chiefly 1999-2004), the first book-form publication of the corpus
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Abulafia, Abraham ben Samuel' (via Encyclopedia.com)
